where: crates/hir-def/src/deps/awaited.rs (deleted), crates/hir-def/src/deps/serve.rs (`serve_asked`, deleted), crates/blaze-lower/src/lib.rs (`lower_awaiting`, deleted), crates/blaze-cargo/src/serve/unit.rs and unit/deps.rs (`asked`, `blocked_ready`, `release`, the serve before the harness; deleted)
what: The awaited crates (5595254297, 2026-11-11: a crate added to the front end has no job until a serve asks the store about it) stopped the smoke project three times with the same error, `no maintained resolution for crate libc .. it waits for the records of crate libc` in unit `smoke-sys (build script)`: once as built, once after a fix of what a serve asks about (19874cb5d7, then the rule moved into `deps::serve` with a check after it), and once more on 2026-11-12 on the head with two other bugs removed. The only build that passes the smoke is the tree with the mechanism reverted (int-good, 7b970bbe0d). The mechanism is deleted, not fixed a third time; the front end resolves every crate in the write that adds it and serves after, as before.
cost: three failed smoke rounds on the build VM, two fix lanes (one briefed on a cause the code did not have, annoyance awaited-stall-1), a five-commit revert branch kept beside the head, and this lane; and the removal gives back what the mechanism saved: every crate is resolved from source once at a restart before the store is asked, and the unserved ones again after each serve that hits (the number on record for that path is reth, 827 crates, 191.6 s; not measured by this lane)
cause: Not found, and not looked for again: by the main agent's trace of the third failure `libc` was read at +19 s while 17 crates were still awaited and no serve ran between +7.9 s and +29.1 s. Read from the code by this lane: a crate left the set only when a serve listed it or a crate above it, a serve ran only where the unit writer called one (at lowering, and at a batch of runs and loads), and a unit began whenever the plane had it ready; nothing tied the plane's readiness to the set.
whys: Why did a unit read a crate that had no resolution? Its crate, or one below it, was still in the awaited set when the unit's build began.

Why was it still in the set? A crate left it only when a serve asked about it, and serves ran at points the unit writer chose (the lowering, a batch of runs and loads applied), not when a unit became ready.

Why could a unit begin before its serve? Readiness is the plane's (the unit graph and `Waits`), and the set was a second answer to `may this be read yet` kept in the database (the crate graph), with its own release events; the two were joined only by a rule in a comment: nothing may read a crate before `serve_asked` released it.

Why was that rule not a type or a node? The feature was added as a fast path on the existing front end (skip the maintainers for crates that will be served) instead of as work the scheduler owns: a held set was the smallest change that kept `lower` then `serve` as two steps.

Why was it fixed twice before it was removed? Each fix widened what a serve asks about (every blocked ready unit, then a check after the serve) without a trace of which write left `libc` awaited, so each was a guess at the same symptom; rule 66's second-fix stop was not applied until the third failure.
class: a second scheduling protocol beside the scheduler: a set of held things with its own release events and a promise about ordering (`nothing reads X before Y released it`) that no type, node or edge of the plane enforces; its mirror is a fast path bolted onto a slow default (rule 66's sign)
prevention: Done in this lane: the mechanism and its tests are deleted in every crate (`Awaited`, `await_added`, `await_crates`, `release`, `blocked`, `blocker`, `serve_asked`, `lower_awaiting`, `Lowered::any_awaited`, `Db::note_crates_added`, `LastWrite::blocked`, `Unmaintained::awaited`, `deps::asked`, `deps::blocked_ready`, the serve before the harness, the `waits` argument of `deps::serve`), so there is one answer to `may this be read`: a crate in the graph is maintained or served. docs/v2/plan/design/restore.md says what was removed, why, and what the removal costs. Still to do, by the end-state design (docs/v2/plan/design/end-state.md): lazy loading of a dependency crate's records is a cover per registry crate that seeds a kernel session when something demands it, so the order is an edge of the plane; the target it has to meet is written in restore.md's F2 note (no from-source job in the lowering's pass for a crate with records, and no change of the whole crate graph at a serve). A guard worth adding with it: a gate check that refuses a new singleton input read by both maintainers to skip crates.
